dimV=dimkerT+dimimT.
(1)
To prove it, take a basis v1​,…,vk​ of kerT and extend it to a basis
v1​,…,vk​,vk+1​,…,vn​
(2)
of V. The vectors Tvk+1​,…,Tvn​ span imT. They are also linearly independent: if ∑j=k+1n​aj​Tvj​=0, then ∑j=k+1n​aj​vj​∈kerT, and independence of the chosen basis forces every aj​ to vanish. Thus the rank is n−k and the nullity is k.
For the given subspace, row reduction of the coefficient matrix gives
​100​010​330​001​43/3−5/3−11/3​​.
(3)
Taking x3​=s and x5​=t therefore gives
(x1​,x2​,x3​,x4​,x5​)=s(−3,−3,1,0,0)+3t​(−43,5,0,11,3).
(4)
Hence
dimW=2​,{(−3,−3,1,0,0),(−43,5,0,11,3)}​

Solution

Words: 128
2E OurBigBook.com
After the 2n sides are identified in pairs, the polygonal-schema Euler count gives one face, n edges and some number V≥1 of vertices. The Euler characteristic of a closed orientable genus-g surface is 2−2g, so
2−2g=V−n+1,n=V−1+2g≥2g.
(6)
For genus two, take a regular octagon in the Poincare disc model and identify each side with its opposite side, with the orientation reversed along the boundary. One cyclic labelling is
a,b,c,d,a−1,b−1,c−1,d−1.
(7)
The quotient has V=1, E=4, and F=1, hence Euler characteristic −2 and genus two. All eight vertices become one point, so smoothness requires their angles to sum to 2π. Each interior angle is consequently
82π​=4π​​.
(8)
Equivalently, the hyperbolic polygon area formula shows that the regular hyperbolic octagon fundamental polygon has area
(8−2)π−8(4π​)=4π,
(9)
as required by the Gauss-Bonnet theorem for a genus-two surface of curvature −1.

∇f=λ∇g,g=0.

One solves these equations and then compares the resulting candidates, including any boundary or singular cases.
Let the base have dimensions x and y, and let the height be z. Measure cardboard relative to the thickness of the front and back. The weighted amount used is
A=3xy+2xz+4yz,
(17)
because the bottom has triple thickness, the two front and back faces have ordinary thickness, and the two side faces have double thickness. The constraint is xyz=3.
The multiplier equations are
3y+2z=λyz,3x+4z=λxz,2x+4y=λxy.
(18)
They imply
3xy=2xz=4yz.

x=2,y=1,z=23​​.

A≥33(3xy)(2xz)(4yz)​=3324(xyz)2​=18,

f[x0​,…,xk​]=∑j=0k​∏0≤i≤ki=j​​(xj​−xi​)f(xj​)​.
(22)
This is the coefficient of xk in the Lagrange interpolation polynomial through the first k+1 data points.
Let pk​ denote that interpolating polynomial. The difference pk​−pk−1​ vanishes at x0​,…,xk−1​, so
pk​(x)−pk−1​(x)=ck​∏i=0k−1​(x−xi​).
(23)
The Lagrange formula shows that the leading coefficient of pk​ is f[x0​,…,xk​], whereas pk−1​ has degree at most k−1. Hence ck​=f[x0​,…,xk​]. Starting with p0​=f(x0​) and iterating gives the Newton interpolation polynomial
pn​(x)=f(x0​)+k=1∑n​f[x0​,…,xk​]i=0∏k−1​(x−xi​)​.

The divided-difference recurrence is
f[x0​,…,xk​]=xk​−x0​f[x1​,…,xk​]−f[x0​,…,xk−1​]​​.

For three nodes, the triangular table is
f[x0​]f[x1​]f[x2​]​⟶⟶​f[x0​,x1​]⟶f[x0​,x1​,x2​]f[x1​,x2​]​

A statistic T(X) is sufficient for a parameter θ when the conditional distribution of the full sample X given T does not depend on θ. For a dominated model, the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem says this is equivalent to a factorization
pθ​(x)=gθ​(T(x))h(x),

A sufficient statistic T is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic: whenever U is sufficient, there is a function h such that T=h(U) almost surely, up to the usual null-set qualification. Thus its level sets give the coarsest sufficient partition of the sample space. In a dominated family with positive densities, the likelihood-ratio criterion for minimal sufficiency says that T is minimal sufficient when
T(x)=T(y)⟺pθ​(y)pθ​(x)​ is independent of θ.
(29)

a OurBigBook.com
A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence in it converges to a point of the space. Let (yn​) be Cauchy in a closed subspace Y of a complete metric space X. It is also Cauchy in X, so yn​→x for some x∈X. Since Y is closed and every yn​ lies in Y, one has x∈Y. Thus the closed-subspace completeness theorem proves that Y is complete.

A={0,2},B={0},r=1.
(77)
Then B⊆E1​(A), but 2∈/E1​(B), so A⊈E1​(B).
For a point and a nonempty set, write d(x,B)=infb∈B​d(x,b). The given Hausdorff distance is equivalently
dH​(A,B)=max{supa∈A​d(a,B),supb∈B​d(b,A)}.
(78)
It is nonnegative and symmetric. If dH​(A,B)=0, then every a∈A has d(a,B)=0, so a∈B=B because B is closed; hence A⊆B, and symmetry gives A=B.
For the triangle inequality, the ordinary triangle inequality gives
d(a,C)≤d(a,B)+supb∈B​d(b,C).
(79)
Taking suprema over a∈A, and then repeating with A and C interchanged, yields
dH​(A,C)≤dH​(A,B)+dH​(B,C).
(80)
Thus dH​ is a metric on H(X). Closedness is essential: if it is omitted, then the distinct bounded sets (0,1) and [0,1] have Hausdorff distance zero.
For singleton sets,
dH​({x},{y})=d(x,y),
(81)
so θ(x)={x} is an isometry. Its image is closed. Indeed, if {xn​} converges in Hausdorff distance to A∈H(X), then for every ε>0 and all sufficiently large n,
A⊆Eε​({xn​}).

Hence any a,b∈A satisfy d(a,b)≤d(a,xn​)+d(xn​,b)≤2ε. Letting ε↓0 gives a=b, so the nonempty set A is a singleton. This is the closed singleton embedding in a Hausdorff hyperspace.
If H(X) is complete, its closed subspace θ(X) is complete. Since θ is an isometry, X is complete. Hence completeness is reflected by the Hausdorff hyperspace.

a OurBigBook.com
The classification of isolated singularities can be stated through the Laurent expansion of f about a:
  • The singularity is removable when f extends holomorphically to a, equivalently when every negative-power Laurent coefficient is zero.
  • It is a pole of order k when (z−a)kf(z) extends holomorphically to a function nonzero at a. Equivalently, the Laurent series starts with a nonzero (z−a)−k term and has no more negative power.
  • It is essential when it is neither removable nor a pole, equivalently when infinitely many negative-power coefficients are nonzero.

μ=me​+mμ​me​mμ​​.

Words: 100 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 100
a OurBigBook.com
Starting from i, the probability of reaching j before returning to i is α. Conditional on reaching j, each visit to j is followed by a hit on i before the next return to j with probability α, by symmetry and the Strong Markov property. For α>0, the number of visits after entry is therefore geometric on {1,2,…} with mean 1/α. Hence the two-state excursion visit law gives
Ei​N=αα1​=1​(α>0).
(166)
In the degenerate case α=0, the chain never reaches j before its return to i, so N=0 almost surely and Ei​N=0.
